58.0.0.en: 1- “Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?”

58.0.1.en: Mute righteousness: righteousness that is suppressed, which is neither proclaimed nor carried out.

58.0.2.en: 1- David the prophet asks the wicked rulers and officials: do they speak righteousness in their judgments? Or do they suppress righteousness and not carry it out, or speak deceitful words that seem right but are false, as Absalom sympathized with the people and their cases, wishing that if he were king over the people he would do them justice? He was flattering his people so that they would love him, and then he rose in revolt against his father. He continued for two years until he had won many to himself, and rose in his revolt and drove out his father David (2 Sam 15:2-6).

58.0.3.en: 2- He confirms his first question of reproach with another like it, asking the officials, do you judge uprightly? For in their judging they gave unjust judgments, as the Jews did with Christ, and obtained an order from Pilate for His crucifixion, relying on false accusations.

58.0.4.en: 3- David marvels that these unjust rulers claim that they judge by righteousness and uprightness, while they wish to kill him though he is innocent, for this injustice that fell upon David reveals their evil and their cunning. And he reminded them of their weakness, for he said to them, “O ye sons of men,” that is, that God the just Judge has all authority in His hand, to prevent their injustice and their evil directed at him.

58.1.0.en: 2- “Yea, in heart ye work wickedness; ye weigh the violence of your hands in the earth.”

58.1.1.en: David makes clear to the unjust rulers that their desire and the intention of their hearts is evil, and then they turn their desire into an act that they do with their hands. They weigh the violence, meaning that they prepare it and know its measure and its weight, and they are aware of the evil they do. This shows their insistence on evil and their persistence in it.

58.2.0.en: 3- “The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies.”

58.2.1.en: David describes these wicked judges as estranged from the womb and going astray from the belly.

58.2.2.en: What is meant is not that they went astray as embryos, for an embryo does not go astray, but that from the beginning of their lives they learned evil from their fathers, and when they grew up they lived in it and spoke lies. This shows the importance of sound spiritual upbringing.

58.3.0.en: 4- “Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear;” 5- “Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.”

58.3.1.en: Poison: the source of venom in the snake’s body.

58.3.3.en: Charmers: the plural of snake-charmer, one who gathers serpents so that they do not bite people.

58.3.4.en: Charmers (chanters): the snake-charmers recite incantations and call to the serpents, to gather them and neutralize their harm to people.

58.3.5.en: 1- David describes the influence of these wicked men as like poison that has no cure, and also describes them as like the serpent that does not hear, because they do not hear the voice of God and stop their ears to Him. On the other hand they do not listen to the cries of the wronged, that is, they are hard of heart, without mercy on anyone, and so they are children of Satan, who is known in the Holy Bible as the serpent that mercilessly brought down the human race. Saul, for example, did not merely pursue David but tried to kill him, like the poisonous snake that kills its victim, and there is no cure for its poison. At the same time Saul was deceitful like the serpent: he first showed his love for David and that he wished to grant him the favor of marrying his daughter, and then asked of him as a dowry the killing of a hundred Philistines, in order to be rid of him.

58.3.6.en: 2- He likens the wicked not only to poisonous serpents, but says that they refuse to respond to the charmers, the chanters, who try to neutralize their poisons; that is, these wicked men refuse to respond to any advice to stop their evil.

58.3.7.en: If only you would respond to the voice of God on the tongue of the Church’s teachers and of everyone who advises you, so that you do not fall into evil, and if you fall into it, do not persist, lest your heart harden.

58.4.0.en: 6- “Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O LORD.”

58.4.2.en: 1- David likened his enemies to beasts with sharp teeth that wish to devour him and tear him, and to young lions with great teeth able to grind his bones, and perhaps he remembered the lion and the bear over which God gave him victory when he was a shepherd of sheep (1 Sam 17:36). If in (v. 4) he likened his enemies to serpents, that is, enemies who fight him with craftiness and cunning, here he likens them to fierce young lions that attack him openly, for David is fought in every way, in secret and in the open, and this shows the difficulty of the war and the extent of his suffering.

58.4.3.en: 2- He asks God to break the sharp teeth, which signify the enemies’ sharp, wounding words, and to break out the great teeth, which signify the enemies’ crushing strength. But above these enemies is God, who protects him and is able to break and remove all the enemy’s strength; therefore David is at peace as long as he prays.

58.4.4.en: 3- This psalm is a prophecy about Christ, who was fought by His enemies with the cunning of serpents, in attempts to catch a word against Him, or attacked violently and sought to be destroyed, as they cried, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Lk 23:21).

58.5.0.en: 7- “Let them melt away as water, let them go. When he aims his arrows, let them turn aside.”

58.5.1.en: Aims: prepares the arrow for shooting.

58.5.2.en: Let them turn aside: let them swerve from their target.

58.5.3.en: 1- David asks God also to blot out the power of his enemies, and likens them to water that falls on the ground in the desert and is swallowed up and vanishes, leaving no trace, that is, the enemies’ power is nullified and does not affect him.

58.5.4.en: 2- David also likens his enemies to arrows that are prepared to be shot at the target, and swerve from it, that is, do not hit David. In this God protects David, however great his enemies’ strength and their threats against him.

58.6.0.en: 8- “As a snail which melteth as it goeth: like the untimely birth of a woman, let them not see the sun.”

58.6.1.en: Snail: a soft-bodied animal that lives in a sea shell.

58.6.2.en: 1- Likewise David likens the enemies to a small sea creature called the snail, which lives inside a shell, and when it comes out of it and finds an enemy it changes its color from red to a pale white, then secretes a sticky substance on which to slide, and reaches its hiding place inside the shell and seems to have melted. So God makes David’s enemies weak, afraid, and they vanish from before David’s face, because God’s power is with him.

58.6.3.en: 2- David likens the enemies with a new comparison, the untimely birth of a woman, that is, the embryo whose growth was not completed to become a child, so it falls from the womb and dies, that is, it does not become a newborn enjoying the sun and the air.

58.7.0.en: 9- “Before your pots can feel the thorns, whether raw or burned, he shall sweep them away.”

58.7.1.en: Sweep them away: drive them before him with force.

58.7.2.en: 1- David gives another new comparison for the swiftness with which the enemies vanish. He imagines pots set on thorns in which a fire has been lit, and before the pots feel the heat given off by the thorns, whether these thorns are raw and unburned, or part of them has burned, that is, before the contents of the pots are affected by the heat given off by the thorns, the enemies vanish, and the storm winds sweep them away, and they are not found. All this shows God’s power, which quickly puts the enemies away from David.

58.7.3.en: 2- The pots do not feel the thorns, whether raw or burned (green or dry), that is, David does not feel the troubling of his enemies, because God quickly puts them away from him.

58.7.4.en: 3- The storm wind signifies the wrath of God, which puts the enemies away from David, whether they are raw, green thorns, that is, having vitality, or burned, that is, in weakness; in both cases they do not stand before God’s wrath.

58.7.5.en: If your God is perfect in His power, do not be troubled by the strength of the demons who fight you, for they are nothing before His power, even if they have made you fall into sin many times. Rise, leaning on God in prayers and striving, confident of your victory.

58.8.0.en: 10- “The righteous shall rejoice when he seeth the vengeance: he shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked.”

58.8.1.en: Vengeance: that is, retribution, meaning by it the wrath of God and the punishment of the wicked.

58.8.2.en: 1- God takes vengeance on David’s enemies; therefore David, that is, the righteous man, rejoices in God’s vengeance, not out of hatred for the enemies or gloating over them, but for the victory of righteousness and the showing of the futility of evil, and in this he remains steadfast in righteousness and in life with God.

58.8.3.en: 2- There was an ancient custom in wars that after victory over the enemies they would wash their feet in the enemies’ blood. David uses this comparison to show the completeness of the victory of righteousness and the joy of the righteous man. This makes David take warning from the destruction of the wicked man, keep away from evil, and tread down all the corruption of the world.

58.9.0.en: 11- “So that a man shall say, Verily there is a fruit for the righteous: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth.”

58.9.1.en: 1- David sums up the whole psalm in this verse, for when the righteous man sees the punishment of the wicked mentioned in (vv. 6-9), he trusts in the justice of God the Judge, who governs the world, and so is not troubled by the strength of the enemies however much they exalt themselves.

58.9.2.en: 2- The faith of David and of all the righteous in God’s just judgment moves them to stand firm in righteousness and to adorn themselves with its fruit, which is the virtues, for they live secure and so advance in the life of righteousness.

58.9.3.en: If only you would look every day to Christ, the Holy and Righteous One, so that you may stand firm in the life of righteousness and even grow in it, and learn from the saints, and so pass through the world and its evils in peace, even with joy.

58.9.4.en: The call to God the Savior. To the chief Musician, Al-taschith (Destroy not), a golden psalm (Michtam) of David; when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him: “Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God” (v. 1) Introduction:

58.9.6.en: 2- When was it written? When Saul sent messengers to kill David in his house, but his wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, warned David and let him down through a window of their house before they arrived, and put the teraphim in his bed, with a pillow of goats’ hair at its head, and covered it, and when Saul’s messengers arrived to seize David, Michal told them that he was sick, but Saul told his messengers to bring him even though he was sick, and when they rushed into the house they did not find him (1 Sam 19:12-14). This psalm is counted among the oldest psalms that David wrote.

58.9.7.en: 3- This psalm was sung by a group of Levite singers who had a leader, that is, a chief.

58.9.8.en: 4- This psalm was sung to a musical tune called “Destroy Not,” or an instrument called “Destroy Not” with nine strings. Some of the Fathers see that the words “Destroy not” also mean that God did not allow David to be destroyed and delivered him from Saul’s hand.

58.9.9.en: 5- This psalm is one of David’s great, precious psalms; therefore it is called a golden psalm (Michtam), and it was written in gold ink.

58.9.10.en: 6- The idea of David’s escape by being let down through the window was repeated in the New Testament when they let St. Paul the Apostle down through the window to escape from Damascus (Acts 9:25).

58.9.11.en: 7- This psalm is counted among the Messianic psalms because David here is a type of Christ: as Saul’s messengers watched David’s bed and thought he was sleeping on it, and then rushed in and found only his clothes, so also the guards stood at the tomb and thought that the body of Christ was inside the tomb, but were surprised by His resurrection, and that there was nothing in the tomb but the grave clothes.

58.9.12.en: 8- This psalm expresses a man who suffers distress, and prays, and the Lord delivers him, and so he praises Him and thanks Him.

58.9.13.en: 9- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

59.0.s.en: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

59.0.0.en: 1- “Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God: defend me from them that rise up against me.” 2- “Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men.”

59.0.1.en: 1- When David felt that Saul wanted to kill him, while he was still living in his house in Jerusalem with his wife Michal, he cried out to God to deliver him from his enemies and protect him from their evil. And since he prayed, he was assured that he had put himself in God’s hand, which is able to keep him and protect him, and God intervened in a miraculous way, for He made Saul’s daughter stand against her father, and Michal said to David, Flee quickly lest my father kill you, and let him down through a window of her house, and he fled without Saul’s spies, who were watching the door of the house, noticing. David believes that it was God who rescued him, using Michal, and this made his faith in God firm.

59.0.2.en: 2- It appears that Saul wanted to slaughter David; therefore David asked God to deliver him from bloody men. The Church asks God at all times to rescue her, protect her, deliver her and save her, and the Lord answers and keeps His Church throughout the generations.

59.1.0.en: 3- “For, lo, they lie in wait for my soul: the mighty are gathered against me; not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O LORD.”

59.1.1.en: 1- David declares how Saul and those with him laid an ambush for him to kill him; they are strong and David is weak, but his strength is in his reliance on God, and because he walks in uprightness he is innocent, and they want to kill him.

59.1.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, whom the Jews tried many times to catch by a word so as to seize Him and kill Him, relying on their strength and their connection with the Roman authority, though He is without sin and they know this, and nothing moves them but their evil and their love of holding on to leadership, for fear of Christ and His popularity, as Saul clung to the love of power and feared the growth of David’s popularity lest he take the throne from him.

59.1.3.en: 3- The mighty are the sinners and the demons, who with cunning and craftiness lie in wait for the innocent children of God to make them fall into sins.

59.2.0.en: 4- “They run and prepare themselves without my fault: awake to help me, and behold.”

59.2.1.en: 1- David makes clear to God that his enemies are crowding together and running toward him, that is, hastening to destroy him. They are preparing the plot to kill him, knowing that he is innocent; therefore he calls on God to look at him and rescue him. Though they gathered around his house by night, he trusts in God, who is able to rescue him; therefore he says to Him, Awake, for they surround me, and do not wait, O God, until the morning lest they kill me. And indeed God moved Michal, and she let him down by night through the window, and he escaped from the hands of his enemies.

59.2.2.en: 2- David asks God to look upon his innocence, to rescue him from the wicked who wish to destroy him.

59.3.0.en: 5- “Thou therefore, O LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel, give heed to visit all the nations: be not merciful to any treacherous transgressor. Selah.”

59.3.1.en: 1- When David felt the enemies drawing near to him to kill him, he cried out to God, in whose power he trusts; therefore he called Him the LORD of hosts, who is at the same time the God of Israel, for His power is for the benefit of His people and His children. Therefore David asks Him to give heed, that is, to prepare to intervene to rescue him from death. And because Saul and his helpers went on in evil in their attempts to kill David, they are like the nations in their evil, and deserve God’s visitation, that is, His calling them to account and punishing them for their treachery and iniquity, for the punishment of persisting in evil is destruction.

59.3.2.en: 2- This psalm is fit to be repeated by the people of God in their wars with the nations around them, since it mentions here the word “nations,” and by it he may mean the nations around the people of God, so he asks the mighty God, the LORD of hosts, the protector of His people Israel, to give heed and call the nations to account and punish them without mercy, for their rejection of God and their persistence in evil.

59.3.3.en: 3- He ends this verse with the word Selah, a musical pause for meditating on God’s power that supports His children.

59.4.0.en: 6- “They return at evening: they make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city.”

59.4.1.en: They make a noise: the voice of the dog that shows its weakness, which is different from the barking that shows its strength.

59.4.2.en: 1- David describes his enemies as like dogs that come at evening and make weak sounds. Men actually came and watched David’s house by night, and they spoke to one another in low voices so that no one would notice them. And they go round about the city of Jerusalem to spy and learn news of David, and to make sure that he is in his house so that they can kill him.

59.4.3.en: 2- The gathering of the wicked in the evening, where there is darkness, shows their inclination to evil that they do in the dark, and they spend their night in anxiety and in devising plots, whereas God gives the righteous man quiet sleep by night.

59.5.0.en: 7- “Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords are in their lips: for who, say they, doth hear?”

59.5.1.en: They belch out: they speak evil.

59.5.2.en: David continues describing his enemies with three things: first, that they speak evil words; second, that they wrong people, for their words wound and destroy, and therefore he called them swords; and third, that they make light of God’s long-suffering toward them, and think that He does not hear their evils. All this means that the enemies went on in their sins, not profiting from God’s long-suffering as an opportunity for their repentance.

59.6.0.en: 8- “But thou, O LORD, shalt laugh at them; thou shalt have all the nations in derision.”

59.6.1.en: David lifts his eyes to God and turns them away from the wicked men’s attempts to destroy him, and sees God in His power deriding all their evil plots, for He is able to nullify them in a moment and deliver His son David. This shows the extent of David’s faith and his trust in God.

59.7.0.en: 9- “Because of his strength I take refuge in thee: for God is my refuge.”

59.7.1.en: When David looked at the strength of his enemies he felt his weakness, so he hastened to look to God, who is stronger than all, and took refuge in Him to protect him from the enemy, because David had grown accustomed to taking refuge in God and being fortified in Him, so that he lives secure however much evil surrounds him.

59.7.2.en: Get used to looking to God at all times, so that you depend on Him, and are not shaken by the turmoil of the world around you, and it is easy for you to seek Him, and He nullifies all the devil’s plots, and when you are at peace you enjoy fellowship with God and service of Him.

59.8.0.en: 10- “The God of my mercy shall go before me: God shall let me see my desire upon mine enemies.”

59.8.1.en: 1- Since David was assured that God is his stronghold and refuge, he began to describe his God with humility, saying that His mercy goes before him, that is, that he lives by God’s mercy, because he is a sinner, weak and falling short.

59.8.2.en: 2- God, who protects David, shows him the weakness of his enemies and how God disciplines them and punishes them because they wronged him, and also guides him how to deal with them, and so David enjoys seeing God and hearing His voice.

59.9.0.en: 11- “Slay them not, lest my people forget: make them wander by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield.”

59.9.1.en: Make them wander: make them stray, that is, be scattered, dispersed and dispersed abroad, and not know their way. Our shield: the shield is a defensive implement that the soldier used in ancient times; it is a piece of wood with a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand, and he moves it before his face and body to protect him from arrows.

59.9.2.en: 1- David asks God not to destroy the enemies of his people, but to make them wander, that is, in weakness, not knowing how to walk or act, and to bring them down, that is, to lower them from their pride, so that they feel their weakness. In this David’s love for his people and for his enemies appears, in the following:

59.9.3.en: a- God protects His people from the enemies who have become weak and cannot harm His people.

59.9.4.en: b- When the people of God see their enemies in weakness, their faith is made firm in God, who is their shield and defender.

59.9.5.en: c- The people of God remain ready for war and for defending their country, that is, they are not careless, because the enemies are still present, but weak.

59.9.6.en: d- An opportunity for the enemies to repent, believe and return to God, and this shows David’s broad heart, loving even his enemies.

59.9.7.en: 2- This verse applies to Christ, against whom the Jews rose up and crucified Him, yet He did not take vengeance on them and kill them, as Peter wanted to kill with his sword those who came to seize Christ, and He told him that if He wished He could ask for twelve legions of angels to fight for Him, but He wants to redeem mankind (Mt 26:53). And after His resurrection He did not kill the Jews, but scattered them in the countries of the world after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, so they became weak, as Cain, after killing Abel, became a wanderer in the earth; for the result of sin is always wandering and weakness (Gen 4:12-14).

59.10.0.en: 12- “For the sin of their mouth and the words of their lips let them even be taken in their pride: and for cursing and lying which they speak.”

59.10.1.en: 1- David identified his enemies’ sins as two sins:

59.10.2.en: a- Their speech, for they fell into sins of speech, such as cursing, that is, abuse, and lying.

59.10.3.en: b- Their pride, for they felt that their plots must succeed, and trusted in their personal strength. For these two sins God took them, that is, called them to account and punished them, so Saul and his sons perished in the war, and the throne passed to David.

59.10.4.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom the Jews rose up with pride and with evil words, demanding His crucifixion, and imagined that they had been rid of Him by His death on the Cross, but the truth is that He rose from the dead and drew them to faith, and they submitted to Him.

59.11.0.en: 13- “Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be: and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah.”

59.11.1.en: 1- In the spirit of prophecy David declares that God will consume his enemies, and he repeats the word “consume” twice, because they will perish on earth, and then in the other life. And by this consuming, that is, when the existence of these wicked men ends, God is glorified in His people, the children of Jacob, that is, those who believe in Him, because He kept His children and consumed the wicked who trouble them, so the faith of the righteous is made firm, and the rest of the wicked fear, perhaps to return, believe and repent.

59.11.2.en: 2- This verse was fulfilled in the Jews who resisted Christ, whom He consumed on earth by the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 at the hand of the Romans, and then He will consume them on the Day of Judgment, in eternal torment.

59.11.3.en: 3- This verse ends with the word Selah, a musical pause for meditating on God’s power, which is glorified in His children and punishes those who resist Him.

59.12.0.en: 14- “And at evening let them return; and let them make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city.”

59.12.1.en: Verse (14) is a repetition of (v. 6), but with another meaning, for it speaks of the wicked in eternity, and describes their life as being at evening, that is, in the outer darkness, and in weakness they make a noise like dogs, and go round about, that is, in wandering, and they remain so for ever in this torment and perplexity, as the position of the rich man in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus expressed (Lk 16:19-31).

59.13.0.en: 15- “They shall wander up and down for meat, and if they be not satisfied, they shall stay the night.”

59.13.1.en: David continues his description of the state of the wicked in eternal torment, that in their wandering they suffer hunger, and remain, that is, stay the night in this hunger for ever, while the righteous are satisfied with the divine love in the Kingdom.

59.13.2.en: Do not rejoice in the gains you achieve by breaking God’s commandments, for they are all temporary and passing, and even call for judgment in the end; and on the contrary, if you fall into sin, hasten to repentance to obtain God’s mercies.

59.14.0.en: 16- “But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble.” 17- “Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, and the God of my mercy.” Morning: early dawn.

59.14.2.en: 1- Although David began his psalm by crying out to God to save him, in faith he ends the psalm by praising the mighty God who saved him from his enemies. And he chants in the morning after his deliverance from their hands and the end of the trial, because God was his refuge. And he thanks God for His many mercies that are hard to count.

59.14.3.en: 2- David prophesies about the resurrection of Christ at dawn on Sunday, “the morning,” and praises the mighty and merciful God, who died and rose to raise His children in Him, and to be a refuge for them continually.

59.14.4.en: 3- This verse applies to the feelings of David and all who believe in Him in eternity, who praise God in the morning, which is the dawn of the new life, and thank His power and His mercy that kept them all their lives and was a refuge for them.

59.14.5.en: Thank God every day for His care for you, and for His rescuing you from the many evils that you know, or from which He kept you without your knowing, and by your praising Him your faith is made firm, and you keep away from sin and enjoy fellowship with Him.

59.14.6.en: God our helper. To the chief Musician upon Shushan. A testimony. A golden psalm (Michtam) of David, to teach; when he strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, when Joab returned, and smote of Edom in the valley of salt twelve thousand: “O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast broken us down” (v. 1) Introduction:

59.14.9.en: a- When the children of Israel were fighting Aram-naharaim, who lives in northern Iraq, and Aram-zobah, who lives west of Aram-naharaim, that is, in northern Syria, and met strong resistance from them. At the same time Edom, south of the kingdom of Judah, struck, so David sent Abishai, and he killed six thousand of them, and then Joab, and he killed twelve thousand of them, that is, they killed 18,000 of the Edomites (2 Sam 8:13). That was in the valley of salt, which is called the Ghor; the valley of salt is a deserted valley lying south of the kingdom of Judah, on the border of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

59.14.10.en: b- There is another opinion that completes the previous one, which is that David also remembered what happened to him when he was driven out by Saul, and when he reigned for seven years over the tribe of Judah, and Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, was fighting him, so David bore much suffering, but God gave him victory, and he reigned after that over all Israel.

59.14.11.en: 3- This psalm was sung to a tune called Shushan (lily), and there is another opinion that Shushan is a musical instrument resembling the lily flower with its fragrant scent.

59.14.12.en: 4- This psalm is considered a testimony from David to God’s help and His power that supports His children. And by this psalm David means to teach God’s children in every generation to believe and trust in Him. The Levites used to repeat this psalm as a congregation with a chief, to teach the people not to be troubled by tribulations but to be patient, to strive and to offer repentance for their sins, and then God intervenes and gives them victory over their enemies, so they thank Him and glorify Him, because He alone is the cause of their victory. How beautiful it is to present teaching in the form of praise and thanksgiving to God.

59.14.13.en: 5- This psalm is a golden psalm (Michtam) of David, that is, one of David’s great, precious psalms, and it was written in gold ink.

59.14.14.en: 6- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms, because David in it is a type of Christ, who bore the sufferings for our sake, and then triumphed over all His enemies the demons by the Cross.

59.14.15.en: 7- This psalm is considered a prophecy about the Assyrian captivity, then the Babylonian captivity, and then the greatness of God is revealed in the return of His people from captivity, the rebuilding of the Temple, and rejoicing in God’s grace and glorifying Him.

59.14.16.en: 8- This psalm suits every person in distress, and helps him to be patient until he obtains God’s victory and passes through the tribulation, and so praises Him.

59.14.17.en: 9- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
